title: Visual perception of materials and their properties
research_question: How does the visual system categorize materials and infer their properties by sight, given the challenges of appearance variation due to lighting, viewpoint, and shape? The paper proposes a general theory of material perception based on 'statistical generative models' as an alternative to 'inverse optics' or 'bag of tricks' approaches.

participants.description: Not reported, as this is a theoretical/review paper summarizing existing research and proposing a new theoretical framework, rather than presenting new empirical data.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Photographs of various real and fake materials (e.g., fruit, wax simulacra, textiles, stones, liquids, foodstuffs).
Computer-simulated glossy spheres under natural (photographically captured) and unnatural (random noise) illuminations.
Computer-simulated glossy reliefs with varying surface depth (shallow vs. deep) and illumination direction (oblique vs. frontal).
Computer-simulated transparent objects with varying thickness and distance to background.
Simulated crumpled materials (elastic and plastic sheets) with varying physical parameters controlling crumpling behavior.

measures.instrument: Adjustment of reflectance parameters, matching tasks
Subjective ratings of appearance (diffuse to translucent)
Ratings of size, contrast, distinctness of highlight regions

findings.mechanism: Visual system can rapidly identify materials from characteristic image signatures.
findings.quote: subjects can identify a wide range of materials from photo- graphs even with brief presentations.

findings.antecedent: Photographs of materials from different categories
findings.consequent: Subjective ratings of hardness, glossiness, prettiness
findings.mechanism: Subjective ratings cluster into categories, suggesting visual judgments of properties enable classification.
findings.quote: subjective ratings of the individual samples were systematically clustered into categories

findings.antecedent: Photographs of real vs. fake materials (40ms presentation)
findings.mechanism: Subjects rapidly identify subtle appearance differences between real and fake materials.
findings.quote: subjects were able to make remarkably precise descriptions of the properties of materials and were above chance performance

findings.antecedent: Increasing skewness of luminance histograms of matte stucco reliefs
findings.mechanism: Visual system uses image statistics like skewness to infer surface qualities.
findings.quote: increasing the skewness of images of matte stucco reliefs made the surfaces appear glossy.

findings.antecedent: Summary statistics (like skewness) derived from intensity histogram
findings.mechanism: Simple image statistics are insufficient to predict perceived glossiness accurately.
findings.quote: subjective matches were poorly predicted by summary statistics (like skewness) derived from the intensity histogram.

findings.mechanism: Illumination systematically biases judgments of surface roughness.
findings.quote: glancing illumination angles make surfaces appear rougher than frontal illumination.

findings.antecedent: Varying contrast and blur of non-specular components of an object
findings.mechanism: Image properties of non-specular components dramatically alter perceived translucency.
findings.quote: varying the contrast (both magnitude and sign) and blur of the non-specular components of an object can dramatically alter its appearance from diffuse to translucent.

findings.mechanism: Visual system can estimate properties of transparent materials.
findings.quote: subjects could match the refractive index of solid transparent materials

findings.antecedent: Thickness of the object and distance to the background (irrelevant scene variables for intrinsic properties)
findings.mechanism: Perceptual judgments are biased by scene variables, suggesting reliance on image distortion rather than intrinsic properties.
findings.quote: judgments were substantially biased by the thickness of the object and the distance to the background.

findings.antecedent: Natural illumination (photographically captured from real world)
findings.mechanism: Visual system relies on characteristic signatures of specular reflection that are conserved in natural environments.
findings.quote: when the spheres were rendered under illuminations that were photographically captured from the real world... subjects were quite good at performing the matches.

findings.mechanism: Gloss perception breaks down when statistical structure of the environment is infringed.
findings.quote: when the spheres were illuminated under unnatural illuminations... performance decreased significantly.

findings.mechanism: Significant 'contamination' between judgments of glossiness and surface relief, indicating complex interactions.
findings.quote: judgments varied significantly depending on the depth of the relief.

findings.mechanism: Interactions between relief and illumination affect highlight appearance, which is used as a proxy for gloss.
findings.quote: most observers perceive the patch with shal- low relief and frontal illumination (bottom left) to appear significantly 'more glossy' than the others.

findings.antecedent: Depth of surface relief (under oblique illumination)
findings.mechanism: Non-monotonic interactions between scene variables affect gloss perception.
findings.quote: under oblique illu- mination, judgments of glossiness first increase and then decrease again as the depth of relief increases.

findings.antecedent: Image properties of highlights (size, contrast, distinctness)
findings.mechanism: Visual system uses highlight properties as a 'proxy' for intrinsic physical parameters, accounting for complex interactions.
findings.quote: a simple weighted combina- tion of these latter judgments accounted for all the main trends in the glossiness judgments

findings.mechanism: Perceived albedo and surface color vary to some extent with lighting, demonstrating limits of constancy.
findings.quote: perceived albedo and surface colour also vary to some extent with the lighting.

findings.antecedent: Room illumination (dark grey room under bright light vs. light grey room under dim light, same average luminance)
findings.mechanism: Visual system uses more features than just raw luminance values to distinguish lightness, reflecting higher-order image features.
findings.quote: observers can distinguish a dark grey room under bright light from a light grey room under dim light, even when the average luminance is the same for the two rooms.

mechanisms: Visual system builds 'statistical generative models' that capture the natural degrees of variation in appearance between samples, rather than estimating physical parameters.

Visual system uses a constellation of low- and mid-level image measurements (e.g., size, contrast, distinctness of highlights) to characterize surface properties, acting as 'proxies' for intrinsic physical parameters.
Perceptual organization mechanisms parse images into salient regions/features (highlights, shadows) to form initial hypotheses about appearance variations.
Visual system identifies key image parameters that vary systematically between samples of related materials and uses these to represent the 'typical appearance' of surfaces.

Visual system relies on statistical regularities in the natural world to identify 'signatures' in the image that are diagnostic of material properties and remain roughly invariant across changes in illumination.
Visual system uses more features than just luminance (e.g., contrasts, filter responses) to distinguish lightness, reflecting higher-order image features and variations.
moderators: Illumination conditions (natural vs. unnatural, glancing vs. frontal, oblique vs. head-on)
Orientation of illumination relative to the surface
Distance to the background (for transparent objects)
Contrast and blur of non-specular components
implementation_implications: Understanding statistical appearance models could lead to more robust computer vision systems for material recognition.
Training computer vision systems on comparably large quantities of training data might yield comparably good model performance for material categorization.
limitations: It remains unclear at what level constraints on image features are imposed, and raw filter responses/intensity statistics may be insufficient for relevant relationships.
The 'true nature' of the visual system's goal (e.g., teleological questions) is difficult to address experimentally.
There is a need to test the ability of hypothesized cues to predict both successes and failures of material perception.
Methods must be developed for perturbing image properties and measuring perceptual consequences to establish causal roles of cues.
Theory must model processes by which the visual system selects which cues to use for material perception.
Material perception research should avoid becoming a 'theory-blind process' of collecting weak correlations.

paper_metadata.title: Visual Recognition
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: What is the sequence of processing steps involved in visual object recognition? We varied the exposure duration of natural images and measured subjects' performance on three different tasks, each designed to tap a different candidate component process of object recognition. For each exposure duration, accuracy was lower and reaction time longer on a within-category identification task (e.g., distinguishing pigeons from other birds) than on a perceptual categorization task (e.g., birds vs. cars). However, strikingly, at each exposure duration, subjects performed just as quickly and accurately on the categorization task as they did on a task requiring only object detection: By the time subjects knew an image contained an object at all, they already knew its category. These findings place powerful constraints on theories of object recognition.

crossref_authors.name: Nancy Kanwisher
crossref_authors.affiliation: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
